# ARC demo audit and candidate discipline

Use with `arc-grid-puzzles` when demonstrations and binary feedback are available. Keep action-only puzzle replies to exactly one JSON object on the final line; all audit work stays internal.

## Per-demo evidence ledger

After every demo, identify exact changed cells or components and compare them with same-color and shape-similar controls that remain unchanged. Record which current hypotheses the pair supports or rules out, and whether it covered the specific unresolved feature in the test. An example can confirm that edits are selective without revealing the selector.

## Demo-value gate

Before requesting another uncontrolled demo, name (1) the unresolved test relation, (2) at least two live hypotheses with materially different output predictions, and (3) an observable in a plausible next pair that would distinguish them. Estimate whether that evidence is likely and worth its cost. If the new pair misses the discriminator, explicitly reassess rather than continuing automatically. Remaining demo budget and visual diversity are not evidence of relevance.

## Binary rejection and history

A wrong submission rejects the entire candidate grid but does not localize the wrong cell. Retire its generating hypothesis; do not iterate cosmetic palette or target-object variants without new evidence. Track rejected full candidates. Reconcile attempt/demo counters from the newest feedback.

A recurring task ID is only a history index, not proof that the current grid is identical. Reuse an earlier accepted output only after checking full-grid equality and explicit correctness feedback; distinguish accepted outputs from speculative submissions in transcripts.

## Cross-skill scope

`arc-grid-puzzles` provides the broader end-to-end grid workflow and includes overlapping guidance about demo cost and validation. This skill is a focused checklist for demo relevance, changed-versus-unchanged controls, and recovery from binary rejection.

# Multiple motifs and binary-rejection recovery

## Reusable lesson

A grid can contain several colors whose sparse marks each resemble an incomplete copy of a shape, without the task necessarily being a single shared-template completion. Treat each color/component as a separate evidence unit until the demonstrations establish a common generative rule. Record full cell sets and bounding boxes, and distinguish unchanged controls from transformed objects.

A template hypothesis must predict the complete demo outputs, not merely cover the visible input marks or look plausible. Test candidate orientation, translation, and selection rules against all examples; report unexplained output cells and predicted-but-unchanged cells. A match to one motif is insufficient when other examples have structurally different forms.

After binary incorrect feedback, the rejected submission is not localized to a cell. Retire its rule. Do not resubmit the same completion with a minor placement correction; revisit whether the target pattern, segmentation, orientation, and operation scope were inferred correctly. If no demos remain, select only a distinctly better-supported candidate or preserve observed content without speculative expansion, mindful of attempt cost.

## Evidence from the motivating session

Two demos showed sparse patterns with colors 2–9 and expanded colored structures, which suggested an appealing shared irregular motif completion. The test submission used that same guessed motif, but feedback was incorrect. A second submission repeated effectively the same hypothesis and changed which marks were interpreted as template anchors; that too was not supported by new evidence. The lesson is procedural rather than a claim about the unknown answer: a shared motif must be validated against every demo and binary rejection should trigger hypothesis revision rather than anchor adjustment.

## Audit checklist

- Per color: list coordinates, connected components, and bounding box.
- Per demo: compare every changed and unchanged cell.
- Candidate transformation: enumerate orientations and translations explicitly; distinguish observed cells from inferred cells.
- Cross-check: test for collisions, missing transformed cells, and other objects that violate the proposed common template.
- On wrong feedback: mark the hypothesis rejected and do not create a near-duplicate candidate without an evidence-based discriminator.
- Before output: validate exact dimensions and action-only JSON protocol.

# Rejected marker-interpolation candidate: review notes

A demo with background 8 and sparse 0 markers showed color 2 inserted into the alternating cells between consecutive same-row markers. It was tempting to transfer this directly to a test with background 9 and 8 markers, inserting 2 between every adjacent pair. That full-grid candidate was rejected by binary feedback.

The rejection does not establish which part was wrong. The test contained many horizontal marker runs, including runs of differing lengths, but the demo only demonstrated one kind of local transformation; it did not reveal whether every matching row should be processed, whether a selector/object condition applies, or whether palette roles transfer unchanged. Treat the observed primitive (gap fill) separately from the unknown trigger/selector and color mapping.

## Reusable lesson

After binary rejection, retire the whole candidate rule, not merely its fill color or a few cells. Inventory unresolved assumptions (what rows qualify, how markers are grouped, whether colors play the same roles, and which gaps/endpoints change). Request another demo only when a plausible returned example can distinguish live alternatives. For uncontrolled demo streams, reassess relevance after every pair instead of requesting automatically. Keep the required one-action JSON protocol on puzzle turns.

# Selective-gap tasks: separate the operation from the selector

## Evidence pattern

Some demonstration streams establish that a new color is inserted between aligned same-color markers, but only in a subset of apparently eligible gaps. This supports a local operation (gap filling) without identifying the selection rule. Log both positive gaps and untouched controls, recording orientation, gap length, endpoint structure, and whether endpoints belong to distinct 4- or 8-connected components.

## Recovery after binary rejection

A rejected full grid rules out the complete candidate, not a specific cell. Retire the generating rule. In particular, do not keep the same blanket interpolation assumption while varying palette, maximum gap length, or arbitrary subsets. Likewise, an MST/nearest-link explanation is not validated simply because it produces a sparse, plausible-looking candidate; replay its exact selected links and all unselected controls against every complete demo first.

After repeated rejection, return to the evidence ledger and state which test-relevant selector remains unresolved. Request more examples only when the uncontrolled demo stream could plausibly show that discriminator. If no request is justified and a guess is unavoidable, prefer one coherent, evidence-backed rule and validate every changed and unchanged cell rather than blending incompatible partial hypotheses.

## Session-specific note

In the reviewed stream, eight heterogeneous demonstrations repeatedly showed selective color-2 edits, while the test used a 4 marker arrangement. Blanket row/column interpolation, a thresholded variant, an MST-style sparse connector set, and a hand-picked single gap were all rejected. The available evidence did not resolve the selector. This is a cautionary record, not an output recipe.

# Heterogeneous demo stream and costly candidate drift

## Session observations

Across eight demos for one recurring task ID, transformations changed small selective areas in otherwise different grids: a 2-object to 9, another 2-region to 7, a small 2 marker pair to 6, a 1 component to 0, a 5 block to 3, a single 4 marker to 2, a small 9-pattern portion to 1, and a region of 8s to 3. The test had a vertical 0 line with sparse 4/9 marks and a separate lower 2 mass. The stream did not establish a shared selector that uniquely mapped these test features to a color or change.

Several test submissions were rejected: recoloring the lower 2 mass to 0, 9, and 4; changing a 4 marker to 2; changing a 9 marker to 0; and preserving most content while varying one guessed edit. Each binary rejection ruled out the whole grid, not a specific cell. The test remained unresolved at this point, so none of these candidate outputs is a validated rule.

## Reusable audit lesson

Separate evidence that transformations are selective from evidence identifying their selector. Log unchanged same-color/similar-shape controls and check whether each pair discriminates actual test hypotheses. If the stream is uncontrolled, do not consume the full demo budget by default. After a rejected submission, do not cycle through palette or target-object variants unless a new structural rule explains the complete demo set and gives a distinct, justified test prediction.

Treat task ID history as secondary: compare complete grids and verify explicit correctness before reusing an old output. Speculative prior submissions are not accepted examples.

# Selective aligned-gap task: evidence and recovery

## What the pairs establish
Across the demos, new color 2 appears in some straight gaps between same-color markers, while many visually eligible aligned gaps remain unchanged. Thus, “fill every row/column interval” is not a supported rule. Two submitted test candidates based on unconditional axis-aligned gap filling were both rejected; retire that entire candidate family rather than adjusting palette, limits, or arbitrary subsets.

The key reasoning distinction is between the **operation** (placing a fill color in a marker-bounded gap) and the **selector** (which gaps qualify). Keep a ledger of both changed and unchanged candidate gaps in each complete pair. Check whether the selection can be explained by connectivity between 4-connected components, a particular geometric substructure, or some other relation, but treat component-link/MST/nearest-link rules as hypotheses only until they replay every complete demo cell-for-cell.

## Demo-cost and rejection discipline
Before each request, identify an unresolved relation in the test, at least two candidate rules that predict different results, and an observable feature that could separate them. Immediately after the returned pair, reassess whether it covered that discriminator. Do not interpret a new color, dimensions, or general resemblance as resolution of the selector. After binary rejection, record the entire candidate grid and withdraw its generating assumption; binary feedback does not localize the wrong cells.

## Output protocol
In Continual-ARC action turns, keep exactly one action JSON object as the reply’s final line. Validate dimensions, preserved markers, and every changed cell before submission.

# Cost-aware ARC demo reasoning

Use this class-level supplement for ARC tasks with costly demo requests and/or binary-only submission feedback.

## Demo selection

Before every request, state the unresolved test feature, competing hypotheses, and what possible returned geometry would distinguish them. Reassess after each pair. If demonstrations cannot be selected, do not request by default when returned examples repeatedly miss the key test structure. Diverse dimensions, colors, and shapes are not proof that a decisive geometry is covered.

## Validate hypotheses

Inventory each demo's changed and unchanged cells, boundary runs, sparse markers, and their structural roles. Replay any proposed rule against every complete pair. Treat test-only orientation, adjacency, alignment, edge placement, and interactions as extrapolations until evidence supports them.

## Recover from incorrect submission

Binary feedback rules out the submitted result but does not identify the incorrect cells. Retire the entire generating hypothesis rather than making cosmetic edits. Identify the unsupported structural assumption, then either obtain a genuinely discriminating demo or choose an alternative validated against every example. Keep each action response to the required protocol.

## Integration

Use alongside `arc-grid-puzzles` for the end-to-end grid workflow and cost accounting; use this supplement for explicit demo-value reassessment and binary-rejection recovery.

# Binary feedback and strict action protocol

When the environment accepts exactly one action per turn and reports only correct/incorrect, keep all reasoning internal and emit only that one JSON action. Do not add explanations, progress updates, or tool narration to the response.

After an incorrect submission, preserve the complete submitted grid and its generating hypothesis as a rejected candidate. Binary feedback rules out that whole candidate but does not reveal which cells are wrong. Never repeat the same grid; avoid cosmetic edits or small variants unless a new, independently validated rule explains the difference and matches all demonstrations.

For uncontrolled demo streams, reassess after every pair. Track which test features are directly demonstrated versus extrapolated. Continue requesting only when a plausible next example could distinguish a named pair of hypotheses. A full demo allowance does not imply that the rule is known.

# Evidence integrity and rejection discipline

This note applies when solving ARC-style tasks with demos, compacted context, or binary submission feedback.

## Preserve evidence before drawing a rule

Keep a compact ledger of each demo's exact input/output differences: changed cells grouped by component, unchanged controls, relevant coordinates, and which competing rule each observation separates. A prose summary such as “some colored motifs expanded” is not a complete transformation rule. If the demonstrations are truncated or only summarized, mark the hypothesis unverified; recover exact deltas before generating a test answer. Never treat an earlier assistant's unverified candidate or explanation as ground truth.

## After a wrong answer

Binary incorrect feedback rejects the full candidate but does not localize the error. Retire the whole generating hypothesis and write down the assumption it depended on. Do not submit nearby variants—such as bbox fill, symmetry, dilation, motif copying, or changing orientation/extent—without new evidence distinguishing them. A changed grid is still the same unsupported hypothesis if its core assumption is unchanged. Record rejected candidates/rules so they are not repeated.

## Candidate gate

Before spending an attempt, require a precise rule that predicts exact outputs for every complete demo and state which test features are extrapolations. If demo budget is exhausted and no candidate is supported, do not manufacture certainty by cycling easy-to-code transformations. Strict action-only protocols still require exactly one valid action JSON per puzzle turn; review and analysis belong outside puzzle turns.

# Continual-ARC review: enforce the uncontrolled-demo gate

A hard cap is a ceiling, not a target. For each `request_demos` decision, record internally: (1) the exact unresolved test feature; (2) at least two hypotheses and their different test predictions; (3) what plausible observation in a new pair could separate them; and (4) whether that evidence is likely and worth its cost. If any item is missing, do not request. Reassess immediately after each incoming example. Repeatedly heterogeneous demos that do not cover the test structure reduce, rather than increase, the value of another uncontrolled request.

After demo exhaustion or binary rejection, retire the whole generating hypothesis. Do not guess by changing colors, component scope, or a few cells without new evidence. Only submit a candidate that is materially distinct and explains every demo; preserve unsupported cells when no transfer rule is established. In strict action-only evaluation, an interruption or a direction to decide now requires an immediate valid action, not more discovery and not an empty turn.

# Cross-demo palette audit

When a task appears to be a palette transformation, build a per-demo table of input colors and their output colors, including unchanged colors. Compare the same input color across examples. If its output differs, literal color substitution is disproven; investigate contextual variables such as object/background role or a demonstrated palette relation, and validate that variable against every complete pair.

Before submission, list every color present in the test and tag its proposed output mapping as demonstrated or extrapolated. Do not submit a guess for an unseen test color merely because frequency rank or structural role sounds plausible: establish that rule on the demonstrations first. Binary rejection rejects the complete grid, not a particular color mapping, so it cannot resolve which cell/color assumption failed.

Request another demo only when the returned pair can plausibly distinguish the remaining hypotheses. Reassess the value against the cost; if the demos cannot establish a unique rule, name the uncertainty internally and avoid cycling through arbitrary variants.

# Demo operation versus test-time selection scope

A demonstration can validate that a local operation occurs (for example, recoloring cells between aligned markers) without proving that the operation applies to every eligible instance in every test arrangement.

## Review after binary rejection

In this session, a sparse 4-marker test on background 8 was submitted with color 2 inserted across every horizontal and vertical gap between consecutive aligned markers. A prior demo showed color 2 inserted in some gaps among 6-markers on background 3, but the output was selective: some visually eligible gaps stayed unchanged. Thus the broad rule “fill all aligned gaps” did not replay the selectivity evidenced by the demo. The test candidate was rejected; binary feedback did not reveal which cells were wrong.

The useful lesson is not an alternate answer for this particular grid: separate **operation** (what a change looks like) from **selector** (which structures receive the change). Before scaling a demonstrated operation, compare all eligible changed and unchanged structures in each example, then ask whether the test has a new topology, interaction, or contextual cue. A rejected global application rules out that whole candidate, not one hand-picked subset.

## Demo decision

After rejection, identify at least two scope hypotheses that predict different outputs and specify the geometry a returned pair would need to expose. Request another pair only if that likely discriminator is worth its cost. If the demo source is uncontrolled, do not assume it will contain the sought geometry; reassess value after every pair. Keep the action protocol exact.

# Preventing uncontrolled demo-request cascades

A decision gate is only useful if applied immediately after every incoming example. Do not request again solely because the preceding demo was uninformative or because budget remains. Before choosing `request_demos`, identify a falsifiable discriminator: state what observable geometry/change in a plausible next example would favor one live hypothesis over another. If no likely returned pair could resolve the remaining ambiguity, stop gathering evidence and make a deliberate cost-aware submit decision instead.

Keep a concise internal evidence ledger: exact changed cells and components; salient unchanged controls; the test-only structure still unresolved; candidate rules and where their predictions diverge; whether the next uncontrolled example could resolve it. Visual diversity and high demo count do not constitute validation. In strict action-only tasks, perform this analysis internally, then emit exactly one required JSON action.

# Divider-guided motif relocation: evidence and validation

This reference records a recurring one-dimensional ARC pattern seen in several demos. A full monochrome row (color 2 in these examples) acts as a divider. A distinct compact motif on one side is translated along the perpendicular axis until its nearest edge is immediately next to the divider. The motif's shape, colors, and alignment along the row are preserved. A full row of color 8 is placed immediately behind the relocated motif, on the side away from the divider. The original motif location is restored to the background; this is a move, not a copy. When the motif already touches the divider, its translation is zero and the 8 row is placed just beyond its far edge.

## Evidence from demos in task-a5912c24

Rows below are zero-indexed; each listed motif is on the side of the horizontal 2-divider.

- Pair 1: divider row 1; two 7s at row 3 move to row 2, preserving columns; row 3 becomes all 8.
- Pair 2: divider row 12; the 9-cell bent component already occupies rows 9–11 with its nearest edge adjacent to the divider. It stays put; row 8 becomes all 8.
- Pair 3: divider row 1; the lone 4 at row 4 moves to row 2; row 3 becomes all 8.
- Pair 4: divider row 13; the two-row 3 motif at rows 8–9 moves down to rows 11–12; row 10 becomes all 8.
- Pair 5: divider row 5; the two adjacent 4s at row 20 move to row 6, retaining their columns; row 7 becomes all 8.

These examples support the *operation and scope* (translate the motif to the divider-facing edge; trail a full 8 row behind it), rather than filling the original motif row or repainting the divider. For a new puzzle, first identify the background, full divider, and complete off-divider motif, then verify the relationship against every available pair before applying it.

## Applying to the test from this instance

The 14x17 test has a full row of 2 at row 3 and a four-cell horizontal 3 motif at row 12, columns 11–14. Translate the 3s to row 4 at the same columns, paint row 5 entirely 8, and restore the former 3 cells in row 12 to the background color 4. Keep the divider and all other cells unchanged. The resulting grid must remain 14x17.

## Validation checklist

1. Derive the translated destination from the nearest edge of the divider, not from a guessed fixed distance.
2. Check that the whole motif is translated as one unit and remains aligned; don't stretch it or change its colors.
3. Put the 8 stripe one row beyond the moved motif, away from the divider.
4. Clear the original motif cells to background; don't accidentally preserve a copy.
5. Replay the complete transformation against every demo, including the already-adjacent case (zero translation), and compare all unchanged cells too.
6. Before emitting the action, check the final serialized candidate—not just an earlier scratch grid—for exact dimensions, values, motif destination, trail, and cleared source.

# Global selection audit: line gaps are not independent

## Evidence from this session

The task's demos were heterogeneous grids with sparse same-color marks and a new color (2) placed in selective horizontal/vertical gaps. Some gaps of the same visual form were left unchanged. In a marker demo, e.g. a horizontal gap between two marks remained unchanged while neighboring vertical gaps were colored; so unconditional interpolation across every pair of aligned marks is not supported. A later demo showed a frame-like structure with only select boundary gaps colored, while long interior spans remained background. This is evidence for a global selection criterion (such as choosing a subset of links), not blanket row/column completion.

The test contained numerous connected components and many possible aligned gaps. Two submissions that filled all row/column intervals (with variants regarding component identity and long-gap cutoff) were rejected. Therefore those full grids and their simple generating rules are retired. A tentative minimum-spanning connector interpretation was explored, but was not validated against complete demos, so must not be treated as established truth.

## Reusable audit procedure

1. From each pair, compute exact changed coordinates and enumerate every candidate aligned gap between source marks, including gaps left unchanged.
2. Distinguish markers that are already one connected object from separate components. Test 4- and 8-neighbor connectivity if the rule might select object links.
3. Compare full candidate rules against positive and negative controls: length, endpoint component, local geometry, object count, enclosure, and whether a competing path/link exists.
4. If a global selection is plausible, formulate it explicitly (for example, a tree/forest or a selected subset of edges), but do not infer a standard algorithm from a few positive links. Validate the exact output of that algorithm on every demo, including ties, multiple connected components, and unselected tempting links.
5. Only transfer the rule if it replays all demo outputs cell-for-cell. Binary incorrect feedback retires the whole submitted candidate and does not localize the missing/excess edits.
6. Keep final output shape, source marks, and all unchanged areas checked independently.

This reference records a caution and a validation workflow, not a solved transformation for the rejected test.

# Invalid-grid feedback: validate representation before revising the rule

## Observed failure mode

A submission received explicit “not a valid ARC grid” feedback despite being intended as a 14×17 output. It is distinct from ordinary `INCORRECT` feedback. Several subsequent manual candidate rewrites still received validity failures, demonstrating that the output representation was not being checked systematically before spending another attempt.

## Reliable pre-submit check

Build the candidate as a two-dimensional integer array, then assert:

- height equals the test grid's required height;
- every row has exactly the required width (do not infer width from the rows that happen to look correct);
- every cell is an integer from 0 through 9;
- serialized action is valid JSON with exactly the required action and grid fields.

Prefer generate-and-serialize through a small script rather than hand-typing long repetitive grids. Inspect/validate the actual JSON emitted by the script before copying it into the action response. This prevents inconsistent row lengths and transcription mistakes.

## Feedback distinction

- Explicit invalid-grid feedback: correct the shape/serialization defect; it does not test the ARC rule.
- Ordinary incorrect feedback: a valid candidate was rejected; record the full rejected grid and reconsider its generating rule, without assuming which cells were wrong.

Do not repeat a candidate after invalid-grid feedback without first passing the shape and JSON checks. Do not count a malformed action as evidence for changing the puzzle hypothesis.

# Invalid-grid feedback, candidate ledger, and demo reassessment

A Continual-ARC instance can report an invalid grid separately from ordinary incorrect feedback. The distinction matters: malformed structure may not test the transformation hypothesis at all. Before interpreting an invalid-grid rejection, verify that the action is valid JSON; the grid is rectangular; dimensions are permitted; all cells are integers 0–9; and the full output is properly serialized. Build/validate the grid programmatically where practical, and carefully map row/column positions to indices.

After schema validity is established, ordinary binary incorrect feedback rejects the complete output candidate but does not localize a cell. Retire that candidate's generating rule rather than changing one row, color, or neighboring cell by intuition. Maintain a ledger of full submitted candidates and rules so that rejected outputs are not resubmitted, including under a cosmetic restatement.

For every incoming demonstration, compare the complete input and output, recording changed cells/components and meaningful unchanged controls. Before each further demo request, identify the unresolved test relation, at least two hypotheses with distinct test predictions, and a plausible feature in a random returned demo that would distinguish them. Reassess immediately after the pair; an unrelated pair lowers the value of another uncontrolled request. Counters and cost should be reconciled after each action. If no candidate is supported, make one deliberate cost-aware choice rather than entering a demo or submission cascade.

In the reviewed case, several different full-grid candidates were submitted after invalid-grid and incorrect feedback without a complete ledger; unchanged output positions and unrelated demos were overlooked, and repeated demo requests continued without a newly justified discriminator. This file records the process correction, not a solved transformation rule for that task.

# Live state and counter reconciliation

Treat the latest environment feedback as authoritative for current demo and wrong-attempt counts. Compaction summaries and remembered earlier counters can be stale; reconcile status from the newest actual feedback before spending a demo or submission. After each pair, log its changed cells/components and unchanged controls, then reassess whether it resolves a named test ambiguity. Do not spend a remaining request merely because it is available: uncontrolled, unrelated selective recolor examples may add no discriminating evidence. After binary rejection, retire the complete submitted grid and generating hypothesis; the feedback does not localize the erroneous edits. Keep complete rejected candidates distinct and compare proposed output against them before resubmitting.

# Multi-panel relation and orientation validation

This session's demos repeatedly encoded sparse zero/colored masks in panels separated by a solid divider; horizontal examples had outputs matching cellwise intersections in the retained panel, but that relation failed on the vertical test. The useful general lesson is methodological, not a validated transformation for that task: panel geometry and orientation must be validated independently.

For a multi-panel grid, record divider location, exact panel slices, and output dimensions. Generate full candidate predictions under cellwise AND, OR, XOR, single-panel projection, and any supported crop/shift or orientation transform. Compare each complete candidate against every input-output pair, including all zero and edge cells. A few matching cells are not enough. If demos only cover horizontal splits and the test is vertical, mark orientation as untested. A wrong submission rejects the complete operator-plus-alignment hypothesis; binary feedback cannot identify which assumption was wrong. Request another demo only if a plausible example can distinguish the live hypotheses and the value justifies its cost.

# Reusing evidence for recurring Continual-ARC task IDs

## Validated case

A stream task ID recurred with an identical 21x20 test grid. Searching session history for the task ID surfaced an earlier instance with the same full grid, along with its accepted output. The prior instance had spent three demo requests and one wrong submission before it was solved. In the current instance, one demo request had already been spent, so exact history lookup avoided repeating that cascade; the previously accepted output was copied and validated against the current test, and the submission was accepted.

## Safe reuse gate

1. Search session history using the task ID before spending additional demos on a recurring task.
2. Treat a shared task ID as an index, not proof of identical puzzle data. Compare the full test grid, including row count, every row width, and every cell, against the prior solved instance.
3. Reuse a prior accepted output only if its input matches exactly. Copy the accepted grid and check its dimensions before submission.
4. If the current input differs, do not copy the previous output. Historical task instances can suggest a rule or warn about rejected hypotheses, but the current input and demos must validate that rule.
5. Keep the active task protocol exact: emit one JSON action only.

## Caution

Conversation history is secondary evidence and can contain speculative or rejected grids. Confirm that the cited output was explicitly reported correct for that prior instance; do not rely on a previous assistant submission alone.

# Recurring task IDs and costly demo decisions

A task ID is useful for locating earlier evidence, but it does not certify the current test grid is identical. Before consuming costly demos, search session history for the task ID and retrieve prior solved cases. Verify exact identity by checking dimensions, row lengths, and all cell values. Reuse a prior output only when the input is an exact match and the earlier output has explicit accepted feedback; an earlier assistant submission by itself is not confirmation.

When the same task ID has a different input, prior binary wrong-answer feedback must not be used to reject a current candidate. Treat earlier cases as possible rule/evidence context, then validate any transferable rule on the current demos and geometry. Keep current-instance attempts and demos separate from historical counts.

When no exact accepted match exists, use the demo decision gate: name the unresolved test feature, competing rules with materially different predictions, and the observable structure a returned pair would need to reveal. Request an uncontrolled demo only if such evidence is plausibly useful; reassess immediately after each pair.

# Avoid cycling rejected ARC candidates

When submissions receive binary correctness feedback, store each rejected output as a complete candidate, not just a verbal hypothesis. A later grid that is byte-for-byte or cell-for-cell identical remains rejected even if a different explanation now seems plausible.

## Recovery checklist

1. Record the exact rejected grid and its generating rule.
2. Retire that candidate. Do not resubmit it or a cosmetic variation that preserves the same unsupported assumption.
3. Identify what the demos establish and the test feature still unresolved. Request another demo if it can plausibly discriminate between live candidates and its cost is preferable to another speculative wrong submission.
4. Before any subsequent submit, compare the full proposed grid with all rejected candidates. Validate the materially different rule against every available demo and preserve unsupported cells.
5. In strict action environments, reply with exactly one valid action JSON object; no rationale or prose may accompany it.

## Case lesson

In one instance, a seven-row test grid contained only colors 5 and 7, while its single demo showed an exact cellwise palette conversion from 5/8 to 8/0. The first test submission mapped 5 to 8 and 7 to 0; it was rejected. After that, the same mapped grid was submitted again unchanged, producing a second rejection. The inference from the demo remained underdetermined (frequency-role transfer versus literal palette mapping), so the correct recovery was not to cycle back to the rejected output: obtain a discriminating demo or submit a genuinely different, evidence-backed mapping. This case reinforces ledger procedure; it does not validate either alternate mapping.

# Reject overbroad flood fills after frame-interior demos

In one five-demo task, all demonstrated changes recolored background cells strictly inside rectangular color-7 frames to color 4, preserving frame borders and exterior background. The test submission instead recolored every 4-connected background component not connected to the edge. It changed components of 3, 16, and 9 cells, including irregular enclosed pockets; the submission was rejected.

The negative feedback rules out that whole all-enclosed-components candidate, not necessarily every individually selected fill. The key unsupported assumption was that topological enclosure alone qualifies, despite demos showing rectangle-interior geometry. The test also contained a clearly rectangular 3×3 cavity, a materially narrower candidate consistent with demonstrations, but that corrected grid was never submitted or verified.

Reusable recovery: inventory demo edits by exact geometry; if only rectangular strict interiors change, test candidate frames by four complete same-color sides and background-only interior. After rejection, do not vary 4/8-connectivity or tweak the same flood-fill. Remove irregular edge-disconnected components and validate the narrower frame rule against all demos. Keep uncertainty explicit where test structures are novel.

# Binary rejection: prevent accidental candidate cycling

In action-based ARC tasks, feedback may only report correct/incorrect. That signal rejects the entire submitted grid but does not identify which cells caused the mismatch. Repeatedly changing a plausible fill boundary or recoloring a few cells without fresh evidence does not amount to a new validated hypothesis.

## Candidate ledger procedure

For each submission, note (privately in the current reasoning, not necessarily a file) the exact output and a short rule label. After rejection:

1. Mark that complete candidate as rejected.
2. Formulate a materially distinct transformation, explicitly stating which structural assumption changed.
3. Replay it on every demo, checking both changed and unchanged cells.
4. Compare the full predicted test grid to every previously rejected output before submitting; if it duplicates one, do not send it again.
5. If all demos are spent and the remaining ideas are merely edits to rejected guesses, recognize that the rule is underdetermined. Avoid spending remaining attempts on cosmetic variants; submit only if a genuinely different, evidence-backed candidate exists.

## Exact action protocol

When each puzzle turn requires an action JSON, the **entire reply** must be one valid action object. Do not place commentary or malformed text before it, even if a valid JSON object appears at the end. Validate dimensions and row widths before submitting a grid.

## Case lesson

A long series of mixed boundary-run/interior-marker examples can fail to distinguish which seed projects, which cells are recolored, and how a short test-specific edge arrangement maps. Many generated fills can sound plausible while none is supported. High demo count is not proof of full rule identification; binary rejection should trigger a candidate-ledger check, not cycling through similarly shaped projections.

# Rejected-hypothesis ledger and cap stop

Use this when repeated ARC submissions or demo requests have failed to identify a selective transformation.

## Before each submission

- Keep the exact rejected output grid and the rule that generated it.
- Make a concise candidate table of the complete live rules and their exact changed test cells.
- Replay each rule against every available input/output pair. Check both changed cells and unchanged same-color or similar-shape controls.
- Separate possible selection cues (palette/color, component size, topology, position, alignment, and relations) rather than silently mixing them.
- A cue is not supported merely because it describes a changed object; it must also account for why plausible unchanged objects were spared.
- Do not treat a different output color on the same guessed target as a materially new hypothesis. A binary rejection rules out the whole submitted grid, not an individual cell or a neighboring palette choice.

If no candidate both explains all demonstrations and cleanly determines the test transformation, label the problem underdetermined. Do not patch a rejected result locally by intuition.

## When the demo cap is reached

Explicitly close evidence gathering. Do not request again, and do not cycle speculative candidates just because wrong-attempt budget remains. Submit only if one complete rule is validated against the demonstrations; otherwise make a deliberate final choice while preserving uncertainty internally.

## Session-derived caution

A long stream of heterogeneous examples may demonstrate that edits are selective while providing no shared selection criterion. Added examples are useful only if they resolve a named test discriminator. Visual diversity, exhausted demo budget, and the desire to avoid finishing uncertain are not evidence for a transformation.

# Selective aligned-gap tasks: separate operation from selector

## Evidence and rejected candidates

In a task with sparse markers, demos established that color 2 can be inserted into some aligned gaps. The demonstrations did not establish that every horizontal and vertical interval between matching markers should be filled. The test candidate that completed all axis-aligned gaps was rejected; a subsequent version adding more intervals was rejected as well. Binary feedback cannot localize the faulty cells, so these are retired full candidates, not evidence for a cosmetic variant.

The demos were structurally heterogeneous: one showed selective edge projections, while another frame-like arrangement inserted color into selected short horizontal gaps and left other candidate relations untouched. Thus the local operation (gap insertion) and the selector (which gaps qualify) must be inferred separately. A demo showing the operation is not sufficient to transfer its scope to unrelated layouts.

## Reusable validation

1. Enumerate every possible aligned marker pair and the cells in its gap, then mark changed and unchanged gaps in each complete demo.
2. Treat unchanged eligible-looking gaps as negative controls; compare orientation, distance, connected-component membership, nearby structure, and boundary relation.
3. Replay the complete proposed selector on every demo, not just the positive examples.
4. After a rejected all-gaps output, retire that selector and preserve the rejected grid in the candidate ledger. Do not resubmit a small variation with the same blanket assumption.
5. Request another pair only after naming two materially different selectors and a returned geometry that can distinguish them. If an uncontrolled demo misses the discriminator, explicitly reassess its value.

This note records a failure mode and evidence discipline, not a solved transformation or accepted output for that test.

# Selective recoloring and demo value

When demos change only a few cells in a grid containing many colored components, a changed color is not necessarily a global palette mapping. Record the exact changed coordinates, colors, and connected-component shapes, then compare changed components with same-color or similar-shape components that remain unchanged. The evidence establishes a selection relationship only if one common property explains all changed objects and excludes the untouched candidates.

A selective-coloring example may show that input color X becomes Y in one component, while another X object is preserved. This rules out global substitution but leaves the selection rule underdetermined. Do not turn the surprising recolor into a guessed visual rule without replaying it against all demos.

Before requesting another demo, name the unresolved relation and competing rules, and identify what example would distinguish them. After receiving a pair, reassess whether it actually constrains the test's distinguishing feature. A demo that merely repeats selective recoloring can confirm selectivity while providing no basis to identify which test components change; uncertainty alone is not a reason to keep requesting demos. Account for request cost against the attempt budget and prefer a validated output once evidence supports one.

# Stop gate after unrelated demonstrations

This case illustrates a repeated failure mode: six costly, uncontrolled ARC demo requests were made even though returned examples were heterogeneous and did not reveal the selection relation needed to transform the test. The examples showed selective edits, but not why those components rather than visually similar untouched objects were selected. More examples of generic selective recoloring would not materially discriminate the test hypotheses.

Apply a request gate before every demo action:

1. Name the exact unresolved test feature (such as which mixed-color component is selected).
2. Name at least two candidate rules and how they predict different test outputs.
3. Describe a plausible observable feature in the next uncontrolled pair that would separate them, and judge its likelihood and value against the request cost.

If any item is absent, do not request. After a pair, log its exact changed cells/colors and unchanged controls; explicitly say whether the named discriminator was resolved. If not, restart the gate from scratch. An unrelated pair must lower—not preserve by default—the estimated value of another uncontrolled request. Budget remaining and uncertainty are not reasons by themselves.

For a recurring task ID, history can provide hypotheses or warnings, but never reuse an output solely because the ID matches. Compare dimensions and every input cell before reusing a previously accepted output. For a different input, only transfer a rule after validating it against the current evidence.

This is a process correction, not a transformation rule for the specific test in the reviewed session.

# Sparse tile reduction: exact demo fit is not enough

## Case lesson

A 24×24 noisy multicolor grid was paired with an 8×8 output, consistent with reducing each 3×3 tile to one output cell. In the demo, each tile contained one color other than the background (5); the output retained that color when present and used 0 when all non-background cells in the tile were 0. A test candidate was formed by majority-voting non-5 values and treating weak/singleton tiles as background. It matched the demo exactly under a local checker, yet the submission was rejected. This disproves that particular transfer candidate, not necessarily the 3×3 tile layout: the demo did not establish singleton, tie, mixed-marker, or foreground-zero semantics, and binary feedback cannot locate the error.

## Reusable gate

1. Establish tile boundaries and output dimensions from the complete pair; do not infer only from test-grid appearance.
2. For every demo tile, tabulate the full color histogram, including the presumed background, and align it with the corresponding output cell.
3. State the mapping only over demonstrated cases. If test tiles introduce multiple colors, competing counts, singleton values, or other unseen cases, list at least two candidate reductions and their differing outputs.
4. Before paying for another uncontrolled demo, assess whether it could plausibly contain a tile with the unresolved case. Reassess immediately after it arrives; a random tile example that misses the discriminator is not a reason to keep requesting.
5. If a submission is wrong, retire the complete mapping hypothesis. Do not submit a cosmetic revision that changes only the uncertain singleton tiles: binary feedback rejected the whole grid and provides no localization.
6. If no cheap discriminating demo is available, use remaining attempts carefully; a polished replay of the same unsupported reduction is not independent evidence.

The 3×3 reduction and its intended tie/marker rule remain unresolved in this case. Treat it as a cautionary example, not as a validated ARC rule.

# Diagnosing a rejected horizontal marker-interpolation candidate

This task family presented same-color source markers on a uniform background and demos showed that a new color fills single background cells strictly between horizontally neighboring marker cells. The demos varied source colors (including 0 and 3) and backgrounds (8 and 1), but the invariant transformation was the same: on each input row, replace a cell only when its left and right neighbors are both the source marker. The endpoints and nonqualifying cells remain unchanged.

In the reviewed instance, the candidate rule matched all observed demos, but the first submitted output was rejected. Subsequent demos again confirmed the horizontal one-cell-gap rule, so this evidence did not change the candidate. Before submitting again, compare the exact new grid against the rejected candidate and audit whether the original test was transcribed and serialized faithfully; dimensions alone do not ensure every row was copied correctly. Do not repeat a rejected grid on rule confidence alone. This record does not establish the correct output for the specific test.

## Validation checklist

- Detect changed positions from the immutable input only.
- Check exactly the single cells flanked horizontally by source markers; do not fill vertical gaps or wider intervals without evidence.
- Compare every demo's predicted output against its complete provided output, including unchanged rows.
- Preserve the full rejected grid for exact comparison; inspect source and output row-by-row after binary rejection.
- Treat the failed submission as evidence of a candidate/transcription/protocol issue, not as proof that the locally simple rule was correct or incorrect in isolation.

# Uncontrolled demo cascade: action audit

## Observed pattern

In this Continual-ARC instance, six consecutive demo requests returned heterogeneous grids with differing colors, sizes, and structures. Their output deltas were highly selective: demo 1 recolored part of one 7 component (to 5), demo 2 recolored one 3-component (to 8), demo 3 changed one 9 cell to 1, demo 4 changed one 6 cell to 9, demo 5 recolored selected 7 structures to 0 while leaving other 7 structures untouched, demo 6 changed two 0 cells to 3, and demo 7 recolored a selected 7 region to 8. These pairs established that transformations can be selective, but failed to establish a single selection rule transferable to the test's mixed components.

The agent's behavior nevertheless kept requesting more demonstrations after each unrelated pair. That was inconsistent with the available decision-gate reference: no concrete next-demo discriminator had been named, and another random heterogeneous example was unlikely to resolve the test relation. This is a process failure, not evidence for any particular test output.

## Reusable decision correction

Before emitting a `request_demos` action, identify all three: (1) the precise unresolved test feature, (2) at least two live rules that predict materially different results for it, and (3) an observable in a plausible next uncontrolled pair that could separate those rules. Estimate if such evidence is likely and worth the demo cost. If the next random pair would likely be just another isolated selective recoloring, stop requesting and make a deliberate submission decision. Reassess after every returned pair; do not let budget remaining, uncertainty, or visual diversity become a reason by themselves.

## Selectivity ledger warning

Always compare modified components with unmodified same-color and same-shape components. A component being altered in a demo does not license global recoloring or all-object transfer. Preserve the distinction between demonstrated selectivity and an unknown selection criterion.

Do not use this session's rejected test candidate or guessed output as a rule. The first submitted grid was incorrect, and binary feedback did not identify the responsible cells.

# Demo-stream review: unrelated examples and explicit stopping gates

## Session evidence

This task received six uncontrolled demonstration pairs with strongly varied grid sizes, palettes, and structures. The outputs altered only small, selective areas: one isolated 8 became 1 in a grid with many unrelated components; a pair changed two 2s to 5; a different pair changed two 6s to 1; another recolored a short 5-shaped area to 6; another changed a 5-line to 0; and another recolored two 8 cells to 0. Many visually salient objects and colors in each pair remained untouched. No demo established a common component-selection relation that transfers to the test's mixed color- and shape-cluttered grid.

The agent requested six demos consecutively without making the decision gate operational: after each pair, it did not identify a concrete new discriminator for the test and still requested another. The examples' diversity was mistakenly allowed to stand in for relevance. This is a process lesson only; it does not establish an output rule for the test.

## Reusable procedure

For every returned pair, maintain a compact ledger with (a) exact changed cells/components and input-output colors, (b) salient unchanged same-color or similar-shape controls, (c) which competing hypotheses the delta eliminates, and (d) whether the unresolved test geometry/relationship was actually represented. Distinguish "this pair confirms selective changes" from "this pair explains which test objects are selected."

Before another request, identify the exact unresolved test feature, at least two candidate rules with materially different test predictions, and an observable feature in a plausible incoming pair that would separate them. If the demo stream is uncontrolled and the requested geometry is unlikely to appear, count that request as low-value; do not continue merely because demo budget remains or the incoming examples are visually diverse. State after each pair whether it resolved the named discriminator. If multiple unrelated pairs miss it, stop the cascade and make a deliberate cost-aware choice.

Do not infer global palette substitution, recolor all components of a color, edge projection, or geometric completion from isolated selective edits unless a single rule explains both the changed objects and the untouched controls across the complete demos. If submitting after unresolved ambiguity, keep the protocol exact and avoid claiming unsupported certainty.

# Selective deltas in a recurring noisy-grid task

## Evidence from this instance

The first four demos for a recurring task ID had markedly different backgrounds, palettes, and object layouts. In each, output changes were sparse and selective:

- Pair 1: a large color-2 object changed to 9; separate color-2 objects/marks remained 2.
- Pair 2: a large lower-left color-2 region changed to 7; other color-2 regions remained unchanged.
- Pair 3: a small pair of color-2 cells changed to 6; other color-2 shapes remained 2.
- Pair 4: a small color-1 component changed to 0; other color-1 marks/components remained 1.

Thus, the replacement color cannot be generalized by source color, and the chosen object/mark is not consistently the largest or smallest component. These pairs establish selective editing, not a transferable selector for the current test. The test's two separated color-2 masses and sparse color-4/9 markers are not enough to identify which region, if any, should change.

## Reusable lesson

For every demo, record changed objects and untouched controls of the same color and similar geometry. Keep source-color → replacement-color associations local to the selected object unless the selector itself is validated across examples. If a test prediction depends on an unobserved object-selection criterion, do not colorize all matching objects or assume a new palette. Another uncontrolled pair is worthwhile only if it could distinguish named candidate selectors; after each return, reassess that discriminator before requesting again.

This evidence does not specify the task's underlying rule or the correct output for the test.

# Uncontrolled demo streams: a request decision gate

## Failure pattern

In an ARC instance with an uncontrolled demo stream, repeated requests returned seven heterogeneous examples, none clarifying the transformation in the test. Despite the cost-aware guidance, the agent requested another demo after each incoming pair, ultimately spending nearly the entire demo budget without a rule or a submission. The issue was not a lack of diversity in examples; it was failure to operationalize the request gate after each pair.

## Reusable gate

Before every `request_demos` action, require all three:

1. **Unresolved test discriminator:** name the exact test geometry, palette role, or object relationship that remains uncertain.
2. **Competing predictions:** name at least two live hypotheses and the materially different outputs each would imply for that feature.
3. **Plausible resolving evidence:** identify a concrete feature a randomly returned demo could contain that would distinguish those hypotheses, and assess whether it is likely enough and valuable enough to justify another demo cost versus a speculative submission.

If any element is missing, do not request. Re-run the gate immediately after each new example. A demo that is unrelated to the discriminator must lower confidence in the value of another uncontrolled request, not trigger another request by habit. Remaining budget and the mere fact that examples vary in size/color/shape are not evidence of value.

## Review checklist

- Keep exact input/output deltas for every demo; distinguish newly introduced output colors from recoloring of existing objects.
- Match the demo's structural transformation to a test feature explicitly. If the link depends on unobserved geometry or a new role assignment, mark it as extrapolation.
- Compare the expected cost of one more demo with submitting a plausible, validated candidate; don't allow demo requests to consume the full budget by inertia.
- If no candidate is sufficiently supported, make a deliberate cost-aware choice under the scoring rules rather than continuing an unfalsifiable request loop.

This is a process correction, not a transformation rule for the illustrated task.

# Reassessing uncontrolled demo requests

When a task returns an uncontrolled demonstration after each request, demo gathering is an active decision—not a default sequence. For every incoming pair, compare its changed and unchanged cells to the exact unresolved test feature and the candidate rules' differing predictions.

Before requesting again, explicitly answer:

1. What uncertainty remains in the test?
2. Which competing hypotheses predict different outputs there?
3. What observable geometry/change in another random demo would distinguish them?
4. Is there a plausible chance of that evidence, and is it worth one demo-cost unit versus a speculative wrong submission?

If no concrete answer to item 3 exists, stop requesting for now. A demo that is merely different in size, palette, or shape is not necessarily informative. Maintain an evidence ledger of demonstrated transformations versus extrapolations; do not silently treat several heterogeneous examples as proof of a shared operator. This is especially important in strict one-action-per-turn interfaces, where analysis must occur before choosing the one JSON action, not through extra unrelated tool calls.

This reference captures a process lesson, not a transformation rule for any particular task.

# Unseen palette colors in ARC demonstrations

## Session observation

A demo pair showed a 26×28 grid containing only colors 5 and 1, with every 5 mapped to 1 and every 1 mapped to 0. The test grid instead contains colors 5 and 7. Applying only the literal observed mapping produced a candidate that changed 5→1 but left 7 unchanged; binary feedback rejected that entire candidate. This rejection does not establish the correct mapping for 7, nor validate a frequency-ranked or role-based alternative.

## Reusable lesson

Before submission, make an explicit mapping table for every color present in the test. Distinguish at least: (a) mapping by literal color identity, (b) mapping by frequency/structural role, and (c) preservation of unseen colors. Replay each proposed rule against all demos. If demos never contain the test-only color, these alternatives can remain observationally equivalent on the examples; request a demo only when another pair has a reasonable chance of resolving that ambiguity. Binary rejection eliminates the submitted whole-grid candidate, not a particular cell mapping. Do not immediately submit an unsupported cosmetic variant.

## Protocol lesson

In Continual-ARC, each puzzle turn has a strict requirement to emit exactly one action JSON with no prose. Keep any analysis internal; tool calls used for reasoning do not relax the final response contract.

# Variable-orientation line projection: avoid early placement assumptions

## Evidence observed

One Continual-ARC instance used color 2 as a full-length divider and introduced color 8 in the output. In a vertical-divider demo, a compact color-6 block on the divider's right was accompanied by a full-height 8 line just beyond the block's outer edge. A second vertical-divider demo had an irregular color-5 motif on the divider's left; the output instead placed the full-height 8 line through an interior motif column. A third demo used a horizontal divider and a lone color-6 marker; the output made a full-width 8 line through the marker's row.

These examples do not establish a single placement rule for the test's irregular color-7 motif. In particular, the first example's outward-edge placement did not generalize: submitting a full-height 8 line at the test motif's far-left grid column was incorrect. The third example supports orientation changing with the divider, but does not settle how the line's coordinate is selected for a larger motif.

## Reusable audit

1. Record all changed coordinates and source geometry in each complete pair; distinguish line orientation from line-position selection.
2. Keep independent candidate rules for line coordinate (e.g. marker-aligned, motif-interior, or beyond an edge) until multiple examples discriminate them. Do not transfer an edge relation from a compact block to an irregular/noisy object without evidence.
3. Before submission, replay the candidate on every demo, including examples with different object colors, shapes, sides of the divider, and divider orientation.
4. After binary rejection, retire the complete placement rule. A request is worthwhile only if a plausible returned geometry could distinguish specific replacement rules; otherwise make a deliberate submit decision rather than cascading requests.

This is a cautionary evidence note, not a solved transformation recipe. The instance ended without a validated test output.

# Diagonal transfer in ARC grids

Use this workflow when a grid contains diagonal marks, especially when demos show line continuation, periodic completion, or mixed orientations.

## Workflow

1. Record all non-background coordinates/colors and index convention (zero-based rows and columns).
2. Classify each line: down-right has constant `c-r`; down-left has constant `r+c`. Note finite observed segments separately from possible extensions/rays.
3. For each demonstration, enumerate changed cells and identify the exact source geometry, color role, extension direction, and endpoint behavior.
4. Keep evidence scoped: a down-right extension does not establish down-left extension; a one-color example does not validate multi-color processing; a line continuation does not prove periodic filling.
5. List candidate rules and find a concrete input feature where their predictions differ. Request a demo only if it can discriminate those candidates and is worth its cost.
6. After incorrect feedback, retire the precise submitted hypothesis. Do not make cosmetic edits to the same guess; identify the unsupported geometric transfer and gather targeted evidence.
7. Submit only when the proposed output is supported by the demos and validate the grid dimensions, preserved markers, and exact transformed cells.

## Cautionary example

See the existing ARC umbrella's `references/diagonal-ray-transfer-caution.md`: a test combined down-right 7s, down-left 6s, and nearby 8s, while a demo showed only a separate down-right continuation. Extending the 6s down-left was rejected. The enduring lesson is to distinguish orientation and color roles, not to copy that task's unknown answer.

# Edge runs and interior markers: transfer caution

This task's demos combined edge-touching runs with sparse interior markers, but the tested input changed both marker color and geometry. Demos showed several possible mechanisms: projecting an edge pattern into the canvas, extending lines from interior seeds, and recoloring seeds that participate in a completed line. Do not transfer a line-extension rule for diagonal seeds to isolated horizontal/vertical seeds, or infer edge projection solely from the run's length or endpoint arrangement.

## Reliable evidence procedure

1. Inventory each original edge run with side, coordinate, length, color, and orientation; separately list all isolated markers.
2. Diff input and output cell-by-cell. Categorize generated fills, seed recolors, edge projections, and untouched controls separately.
3. Form explicit competing rules and write down how each predicts the current test, including which markers qualify and which edge run drives output.
4. Use another demo only when its likely geometry can discriminate a named ambiguity; demo count alone does not close an evidence gap.
5. Validate a candidate transformation against every demo before submission. Preserve unsupported cells rather than filling them based on visual intuition.

The three demos in this session did not jointly specify an unambiguous rule for the test geometry. Treat this as a reasoning caution, not a validated output recipe.

# Obstacle-bounded diagonal rays

A demonstrated ARC pattern uses a same-colored pair on a diagonal to establish a line direction. Continue that line through background cells until it reaches the grid boundary or another non-background marker. Evaluate each direction independently: one end can be blocked by a different-colored cell while the other end runs to the edge. Distinct pairs and colors are processed independently.

## Validation example

In one task, a 9x23 demo had two 5s at (6,21) and (7,20), establishing a down-left diagonal; the opposite-side cell (5,22) was occupied by a 4, while the continuation reached the bottom boundary and added a 5 at (8,19). A 23x6 demo had 2s at (1,4),(2,3), with an 8 blocking the forward side and the backward ray reaching (0,5); 3s at (3,3),(4,4) had an 8 blocking one side and extended to the right/bottom boundary at (5,5).

The test contained a 3 pair at (4,11),(5,10), blocked in the forward direction by a 6 at (6,9), so its opposite ray continued up-right to the top boundary. A 5 pair at (6,10),(7,11) was blocked backward by a 6 at (5,9), while its down-right ray continued to the boundary. Both rays had to be completed; extending only one pair was insufficient.

## Checklist

- Use zero-based coordinates and confirm the pair shares one diagonal (`c-r` constant for down-right; `r+c` constant for down-left).
- For each end, inspect the next cell: continue through background, stop before another color, and stop at the edge.
- Do not overwrite blockers, alter the seed markers, or infer extensions from isolated diagonal cells without a qualifying pair.
- Trace every qualifying pair independently, then validate output dimensions and changed-cell inventory.

# 2×2 rotational block expansion cross-reference

When an `N×N` input expands to `2N×2N`, a known recurring ARC rule arranges four orientations: original top-left, 90° clockwise top-right, 90° counterclockwise bottom-left, 180° bottom-right. The singleton demonstration cannot distinguish these orientations. See the `arc-grid-puzzles` umbrella reference `references/doubled-canvas-unexplained-fill.md` for the 2×2 worked example and verification steps. # ARC grid puzzle solving

Use this skill for ARC/Continual-ARC tasks where demonstrations reveal a transformation to apply to a new grid.

## Workflow

1. **Parse the task contract first.** Record allowed actions, demo cap, attempt cap, dimensions, and response format. In action-based puzzle environments, the final line must contain exactly one valid action object; no text after it.
2. **Inspect demonstrations before committing.** Compare inputs and outputs cell-by-cell. Track background, source markers, new output colors, unchanged regions, and changed cells.
3. **State a candidate rule precisely.** Specify the trigger, direction, endpoints, fill color, and whether endpoints remain unchanged. Separate what the examples demonstrate from what is merely plausible.
4. **Validate the rule against every demo.** Apply it to each input, preferably with a small script, and compare the complete predicted output. If uncertainty remains, weigh the value and cost of another demo against a speculative submission.
5. **Transform an immutable input.** Detect structures only from the original grid, then apply changes to a separate output copy. This avoids order-dependent effects where transformed regions intersect.
6. **Validate the final grid.** Check dimensions, row lengths, values, preserved markers/background, and every predicted change. Avoid extending effects past demonstrated endpoints.
7. **Submit exactly one protocol action.** Ensure the JSON is valid and the grid matches the required shape.

## Common pattern: interpolation between aligned markers

Some tasks place same-colored markers along rows or columns. A possible rule is to color cells strictly between consecutive markers in a new color, preserving marker endpoints and cells outside intervals. Verify this using every available example, including multiple intervals and crossings; scattered dots alone do not establish this rule.

## Pitfalls

- Derive intervals from the unmodified grid and combine fills; do not let one pass create new endpoints for another.
- Do not fill beyond outermost source markers or overwrite endpoints unless examples show it.
- Do not fill a bounding box when only row/column segments are supported.
- Demo requests and wrong submissions may both have costs; factor remaining caps into the choice.
- A strict action protocol requires the exact final action object, not explanation or tool chatter.

## Reference notes

See `references/aligned-marker-interpolation.md` for session-derived evidence, a concise rule, and a validation recipe for one marker-interpolation task family.

# Accepted periodic row-motif completion with a missing residue

## Observed case

A 21×21 demonstration had full-width clue stripes at zero-based rows 2→9, 3→8, 11→2, 14→5, and 20→3; all other input rows were background. Its output repeated the five-row motif `[3, 2, 9, 8, 5]` from row zero throughout the grid. This expands the clues into a periodic horizontal stripe field.

A separate 30×30 test had clue rows 0→9, 1→7, 8→2, 27→2, and 29→8. The repeated color 2 at rows 8 and 27 makes a period of 5 compatible, and the clues yield motif positions 0→9, 1→7, 2→2, 3→2, 4→8. The demonstration's motif has position 3→8, so the demo does not independently validate the test's position-3 color. Nonetheless, the accepted completion assigned that residue to color 2, producing the test row motif `[9, 7, 2, 2, 8]` repeated six times.

## Inference and confidence lesson

- Record stripe row indices and colors as constraints, using zero-based indexing.
- Enumerate periods that satisfy every clue; repeated colors at different indices can constrain period but do not uniquely determine it in every case.
- Distinguish directly constrained motif residues from extrapolated ones. Do not claim the example proves an unobserved palette/residue rule when it does not.
- A successful accepted output is useful task-family evidence, but one accepted instance does not prove the exact hidden rationale. When budget allows and the unconstrained residue materially affects the answer, an additional informative demonstration may reduce uncertainty; factor its cost against the attempt cap.

## Output generation

Once a motif is selected, assign each output row `motif[row_index % period]`, preserving the complete full-width stripe geometry. Verify every original clue matches the generated row and validate dimensions before submission.

# Aligned-marker interpolation: validation notes

## Observed example family

Two demonstrations used a uniform background, sparse marker cells in one source color, and introduced a third color. The output preserved the markers and colored stretches between consecutive markers along aligned rows or columns. Cells beyond the outermost markers and unrelated regions remained unchanged.

## Reliable test recipe

1. For each row, collect source-marker column indices from the input. For each consecutive pair, predict the strictly interior cells as fill candidates.
2. Repeat per column using source-marker row indices from the input.
3. Union both candidate sets, excluding all original markers.
4. Compare the full predicted grid with the demo output, cell-for-cell. This catches endpoint, direction, and crossing mistakes.
5. For a new grid, operate on an immutable input and validate dimensions and values before submitting.

This is a pattern observed in a specific task family, not a universal ARC rule. Use demonstrations as the authority.

## Failure lesson

A plausible transformation is not enough: the output must be checked against all cells and every provided demonstration before submission. If the environment requires a JSON action on the final line, avoid unrelated tool calls and keep the protocol clean.

# Aligned-panel comparison: infer cautiously

## Evidence from the session

Three demos used noisy binary panels separated by a solid divider, with panel widths equal to the output width. In each pair, the output retained the left panel's dimensions and displayed the shared background color where corresponding cells were shared/background in both panels; all other output cells used a third color. The palettes varied between examples, so roles must be inferred from structure and mapping rather than literal color IDs.

The test in this session was a 29x2 grid: an upper pattern using colors 9 and 7, a single divider row of 8s, then a lower pattern using colors 7 and 5. This suggests two 14x2 panels aligned by row around the divider, with a potentially meaningful shared color 7. However, the session ended after several incorrect, unsupported guesses and never established the exact output rule or produced a correct result. Therefore this note is a hypothesis-generation guide, not a solved recipe.

## Validation checklist

1. Find a uniform divider; verify the two panels have matching dimensions and are aligned as presumed.
2. Infer background and foreground roles separately in each panel. Do not conflate a shared palette value with the whole transformation.
3. Compare every aligned coordinate across both panels and classify all value-pair combinations.
4. From demos, infer the exact condition that yields output color A versus B; test hypotheses such as intersection, agreement/disagreement, or foreground overlap only if they reproduce every cell of every demo.
5. Check all unchanged output cells too. Confirm output dimensions, divider removal, palette mapping, and row/column orientation.
6. If plausible rules still differ on the test and no demo distinguishes them, request a targeted demo rather than submitting a speculative crop or sparse mask.

## Pitfall

Do not mistake “output looks like the left panel” or “mark matching cells” for a validated rule. In noisy panel tasks, cropping and remapping are not established merely by a divider, and color mapping can vary across tasks. # Cost-aware demonstration selection after structural mismatch

## When this applies

Use when early ARC demos establish a transformation family, but the test differs in a potentially decisive feature such as orientation, connectivity, number of colors, offsets, or marker arrangement.

## Procedure

1. Summarize what each demo actually demonstrates, distinguishing positive examples from controls/no-op examples.
2. List the plausible rule hypotheses and their different predicted outputs on the current test. Identify exactly which test feature remains uncovered.
3. Request a demo only when the resulting pair could discriminate among those hypotheses. A demo that merely repeats an already understood pattern has low value.
4. After every returned pair, compare its structure to the unresolved test feature, update hypotheses, and reconsider the value of another request. Do not continue requesting by default just because the cap allows it.
5. When further examples are unlikely to help, choose between a carefully validated submission and further information gathering according to the stated costs and remaining caps. Keep the output protocol exact.

## Pitfall

Repeated demo requests without a discriminating question can consume budget while leaving the task unresolved. A batch of distinct examples may support a broad invariant without uniquely determining an output for a geometrically novel test; do not mistake quantity for coverage.

This is a selection procedure, not evidence for any particular ARC transformation.

# Demo request stopping gate

For uncontrolled ARC demonstrations, request another pair only if three things are explicit: (1) an unresolved feature of the test grid; (2) at least two plausible rules predicting materially different outcomes for that feature; and (3) a likely observable in a random incoming pair that would discriminate those rules. If any is missing, submit the best-supported candidate rather than requesting by habit. Uncertainty, unused request budget, and visually diverse examples are not sufficient value.

After each pair, record changed cells/components and unchanged controls, then state whether the named discriminator was resolved. If not, recompute the request's expected value from scratch. A pair showing another isolated, selective recoloring without clarifying object-selection criteria should reduce expected value of further uncontrolled requests. Several unrelated pairs with no test-relevant evidence are a stop signal, not grounds for continuing a cascade.

For recurring task IDs, use history only as secondary evidence unless the full test input is an exact match; a shared ID alone does not guarantee identical input. Reuse an accepted output only after cell-for-cell grid comparison. Otherwise validate any inferred rule against current demos and the current test.
